huntNo.title: Hunt for the no
huntNo.summary: Most people find it easier to say no than yes. A yes is a commitment. A no feels safe and keeps them in control. So word the question so that “no” is the answer you want.
why: People protect their freedom to choose. Push for a yes and they push back. Invite a no and they relax.
A “no” to a negative question means “yes” to your request: “Would it be unreasonable…?” “No, it wouldn’t.”
It makes the next step feel like their idea, so they agree faster and mean it.
And if the real answer is no, you find out early and honestly.
formula: Start soft: “Would it be…”, “Is it…”, “Are you against…”
Use a word that makes “no” the easy answer: unreasonable, crazy, a bad idea, out of the question, opposed.
Ask for one small, specific thing: a site visit, 15 minutes, a short email, an introduction.
Say it curious and slightly unsure, with a downward tone. Then stop talking.

answers.you: Take the yes: “Brilliant, thank you. How does Thursday at 10 look?”
Move to the detail: “Great. Is morning or afternoon better for you?”
Respect it and explore: “Fair enough. What would make it unreasonable?”
Find the gap: “That’s fair. What would you need to know to be comfortable?”
Wait. Count to five. They are thinking, not leaving.

mistakes: Using it for something that isn’t actually reasonable. They will feel it.
Sounding sarcastic or clever. Be genuinely curious.
Filling the silence. Ask, then stop.
Stacking two questions in one. One small ask at a time.
Pushing after a real “yes, it would be”. Respect it, ask what would change it, and move on.
huntNo.honesty: This only works if the ask is genuinely reasonable and you are genuinely fine with either answer. If they say no (meaning no), thank them and ask what would change that.

tonality.intro: How you say it matters as much as what you say. The goal of every call is to get the prospect to say the problem out loud, in their own words. Tone and pace make that feel safe.

tones.name: Curious
tones.how: Relaxed, a little slower than normal, a gentle downward tone at the end. Sound like you honestly want the answer, not like you are reading a form.

tones.name: Warm and reasonable
tones.how: Smile as you speak. Steady pace. Land softly on “fair?” or “OK?” so it sounds like a reasonable person asking a reasonable thing.
tones.example: “Can I take 30 seconds, and you tell me if it’s not relevant? Fair enough?”

tones.name: Certain
tones.when: Saying who you are, confirming a next step
tones.how: Down-inflect at the end of statements. No up-tick, no “um”, no apology. Certainty is what makes you easy to trust.

tones.name: Concerned
tones.how: Lower in pitch, slower, a little quieter. Sound sincerely interested in what the problem does to them.
tones.example: “What did that end up costing you?”

tones.name: Matter-of-fact, no pressure
tones.when: Permission to say no, closes, brush-offs
tones.how: Flat, unbothered and in no hurry. You have no attachment to the answer, so either answer is fine.
tones.example: “If it’s not for you, just say so and I’ll leave you alone.”

tones.name: Upbeat
tones.how: A little brighter and slightly quicker, then settle back down. Never stay high through the questions.

pacing: Slow down on the first sentence. Most people rush the opener, and rushing sounds like a script.
After every question, count two to three seconds in your head. Silence is not your enemy.
Slow down and drop your voice on the important words: the problem, the cost, the consequence.
Go a little quicker on throwaway words (“it’s [Rep]”) and slower on the ask.
Match their pace first. If they’re brisk, be crisp. If they’re slow, don’t rush them.
End statements with a downward tone. A rising tone turns a statement into a question and signals doubt.
After “fair enough?” or “sound fair?”, stop talking and let them answer.
Swap “um”, “just” and “sort of” for a pause. Pauses sound confident; fillers sound unsure.
Stand up and smile when you dial. Your voice changes, and so does your confidence.

microAgreements.intro: A micro-agreement is a tiny, easy “yes” that keeps the prospect in control and builds momentum. Get three small yeses before you ask for anything bigger.
lines: Am I on the right track?
sequence: “I’ll be honest, this is a cold call. Is it OK if I tell you why I rang?” (yes)
“I’m guessing you get a lot of these. Is that fair?” (yes)
“If it’s not relevant, you tell me and I’ll go. Sound fair?” (yes)
“Then can I ask two quick questions?”

objectionLoop.intro: Never argue with a brush-off. Loop back to the problem, up to three times, and change the angle each time.
steps: Label: “Sounds like it’s full on.” “Sounds like you’re happy with them.”
Ask one calm question that gets them to say the problem: “If there was one thing you could change, what would it be?”
Check, with permission to say no: “Is that right?” “Sound fair?”
If they still push back, loop with a different angle. After three, thank them and go.

drills: Say the same opener three ways: rushed, warm and slow, and flat. Record yourself and pick the one you’d answer.
Read five situation questions aloud with a three-second pause after each. Count it out.
Take a brush-off, reply with “fair enough” plus a label, then stop talking for three seconds.
Say a statement, then the same words as a question. Notice the pitch. Aim for statements to fall.
Run a two-minute call where you may only ask questions and say “fair enough”.
mistakes: Rising tone on statements, so everything sounds like a question.
Rushing the opener and the reason for the call.
Filling the silence after a question.
Sounding sarcastic when you label (“sounds like you’re happy with them…”). Mean it, or don’t say it.
The same tone for every stage. Match the tone to the stage.
Reading the line instead of saying it. Know it, then say it in your own voice.

principles: Treat LinkedIn like a networking event, not a cold-call list. You’re meeting people, not harvesting them.
Make connection notes and messages about them — something of value to the prospect, not a pitch about you.
Your own content should help, teach or inspire. Never pitch in a post.
Show some personality: stories, analogies and site photos are what people remember.
What you share matters more than when you share it. A great post at an odd time beats a poor one at the “right” time.
Engage the wider buying team — engineering, facilities, ops, procurement — not just one champion.
Be consistent. 15–30 minutes a day beats a burst once a month.
Sharing a company post is fine now and then, but it never replaces connecting, commenting and reaching out when the time is right.

routine.label: Connect
routine.text: Send 5–10 personalised connection requests to relevant people at your target sites.

routine.label: Comment
routine.text: Leave 2–3 thoughtful comments on posts from prospects, their company or industry voices. A real question beats “great post”.

routine.label: Reply
routine.text: Reply to every comment on your own posts, same day.

routine.label: Reach out
routine.text: Message people when there’s a reason (a trigger), not on a timer. See the trigger list.

routine.label: Log it
routine.text: Tap Log in the app, then update Pipedrive.

triggers.label: New role or promotion
triggers.when: They post or LinkedIn shows a job change.
triggers.action: Congratulate in a comment, connect if you haven’t, then message after a few days.

triggers.label: They accepted your connection
triggers.action: Thank them and ask one curious question. No pitch.

triggers.label: They posted something relevant
triggers.when: Comment the same day; message 1–2 days later if they replied.
triggers.action: Comment first. Move to a message only if the post links to a real problem.

triggers.label: Company news: expansion, new site, project
triggers.when: Within a week of the announcement.
triggers.action: Message about the practical challenge the news creates (shutdowns, live-site working, energy).

triggers.label: They’re hiring engineers or facilities staff
triggers.action: A stretched team often means open problems. Ask, don’t assume.

triggers.label: They liked or commented on your post
triggers.action: Thank them and ask how it relates to their site.

triggers.label: They viewed your profile
triggers.action: Send a short, low-pressure message asking what they’re looking at.

triggers.label: Work anniversary or award
triggers.action: A short human message. Keep it light and move on.

profile.intro: People check your profile before they accept, reply or take your call. It should say who you help, what you do and what changes for them.
headlines: [Your role] | I help [who] deliver [what] without stopping production
[Your role] | HVAC, process cooling and heating projects in live environments | [sector] sites
[Your role] | Helping engineering and facilities teams get off gas and cut energy costs
about: Who you help: “I work with [engineering directors, facilities and operations teams] at [sector] sites.”
The problem: “They need [heating, cooling or HVAC work] done without stopping production or putting people at risk.”
How you work: “We specialise in complex projects in live environments — planning around shutdowns, phasing the work and keeping the site running.”
Proof: one short result with a number or a clear outcome.
Invite: “If you’re planning [type of project], send me a message — I’m happy to be a sounding board.”
checklist: Clear, friendly photo (on site is great).
Banner image of real work plus a one-line promise.
Headline says who you help and what you do — not just your job title.
About section follows the five lines above (short paragraphs, first person).
Featured: a project photo set, a case study or your best post.
Experience bullets describe results, not tasks.
Ask for two recommendations from people you’ve worked with.
Custom profile URL and “open to messages” on.

weekly.text: Reach out to anyone with a trigger.
Question to your network, then reply to every comment.

mistakes: Sharing company posts with no comment.
Sending the same copy-and-paste message to everyone.
Only posting about the company; never about the customer’s problems.
Leaving comments like “great post” or “well done”.

pipedrive.reminder: Ensure you update Pipedrive to keep track.
workflow: Log each touch in the app as you go: one tap, a name and a quick note. No Pipedrive while you’re dialling.
Finish your block (a power hour works well).
Open the wrap-up sheet. Copy each line into Pipedrive and tick it off.
Pipedrive is the record. The app is your scoreboard and your scripts.
checklist: Log the call, email or LinkedIn touch against the person.
Move the deal or person to the stage that matches their rung on the ladder.
Add the next step and a date — never leave a deal without one.
Add notes: pain, timing, who else is involved.
Add any colleagues you’ve found (mushrooming) as new people.

stages.label: Opener
stages.hint: Call out the elephant — say the obvious thing out loud.
stages.delivery: Warm and unhurried. Smile, slow down, land the last word downward.

stages.label: Micro-contract
stages.hint: Get a small “yes” before you carry on.
stages.delivery: Easy and reasonable. Ask, then stop and let them answer.

stages.label: Reason for the call
stages.hint: Short, no pitch. Make “no” a safe answer.
stages.delivery: Matter-of-fact, no pitch. Slow on the three problems; pause before the last line.

stages.label: Situation questions
stages.delivery: Curious and relaxed. Ask, pause two to three seconds, no filler.

stages.label: Problem awareness
stages.hint: Let them say what is not working.
stages.delivery: Lower and slower. Soft downward tone. Let the silence do the work.

stages.label: Consequence
stages.hint: Go one level deeper than feels comfortable.
stages.delivery: Concerned and sincere. Slow down on the cost. Don’t rescue them from the pause.

stages.label: Name the feeling
stages.hint: Use any time they sound sceptical, rushed or fed up.
stages.delivery: Gentle and empathic. Downward tone, then stop talking.

stages.label: Solution awareness
stages.hint: Let them describe what “fixed” looks like.
stages.delivery: Warm and forward-looking, slightly brighter. Let them paint the picture.

stages.label: Decision & timing
stages.hint: Who, how and when. Find out before you ask for the meeting.
stages.delivery: Calm and routine, like checking the diary. No pressure in your voice.

stages.label: Hunt for the no
stages.hint: Ask so that “no” means yes. Then stop talking.
stages.delivery: Curious and a little unsure. Down-inflect, then stop talking and let them say “no”.

stages.label: Close for the meeting
stages.hint: Ask for the meeting. “No” is OK.
stages.delivery: Steady and certain, but relaxed about “no”. Down-inflect on the ask.

warmStages.label: Warm opener
warmStages.delivery: Warm and unhurried. Smile, slow down, land the last word downward.

warmStages.label: Bridge
warmStages.hint: Re-open the thread and agree it is OK to continue.
warmStages.delivery: Friendly and familiar, like picking up a conversation.

warmStages.label: Deepen: situation
warmStages.delivery: Curious and relaxed. Ask, pause two to three seconds, no filler.

warmStages.label: Deepen: problem
warmStages.delivery: Lower and slower. Soft downward tone. Let the silence do the work.

warmStages.label: Deepen: consequence
warmStages.delivery: Concerned and sincere. Slow down on the cost. Don’t rescue them from the pause.

warmStages.label: Deepen: solution
warmStages.delivery: Warm and forward-looking, slightly brighter. Let them paint the picture.

warmStages.label: Deepen: decision & timing
warmStages.hint: Reuse the decision and timing questions.
warmStages.delivery: Calm and routine, like checking the diary. No pressure in your voice.

brushoffs.objection: I’ve never heard of you / are you big enough?
brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: Fair enough, we’re not a household name. That’s partly why I’m calling: to find out whether there’s anything we could help with. Is it OK if I ask two quick questions?
That’s a fair concern. What would you want to see from a contractor to feel comfortable they can handle the job?

brushoffs.delivery: Calm and curious, never defensive. Pause after “compared with what?”

responses.text: I hear you. Out of curiosity, expensive compared with what?
Fair enough. When a job goes wrong on a live site, what does that cost you?
That’s fair. We haven’t discussed a price yet. What would you need to see to know it was worth it?

brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: That’s great. Where do you tend to need extra hands or specialist kit?
Makes sense. What happens when a job’s bigger than the team can handle in the shutdown window?

brushoffs.objection: Come back when we’ve got a project
brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: Happy to. How will I know when that’s happening, and who decides?
Fair enough. What usually triggers a project here: a failure, a budget cycle or a target?
No problem. Would it be OK to check in every few months, or would you rather I didn’t?

brushoffs.objection: Why should I talk to you?
brushoffs.delivery: Light, honest and unbothered. A little humour helps. Don’t get defensive.

responses.text: Honestly, you probably shouldn’t, unless one of those three things sounds familiar. Does any of it?
Fair question. I’ve got no idea if I can help, and that’s what I’d like to find out. Is it OK to ask two questions?

brushoffs.objection: We tried that and it didn’t work
brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: I appreciate you telling me. What did you try, and what happened?
That’s frustrating. What would you want to be different this time?

brushoffs.objection: Now’s not a good time of year
brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: Understood. Sounds like it’s a busy period. When does it ease off?
Fair enough. Is it that it’s a busy time, or that this isn’t on your list right now?

brushoffs.objection: Can you call my colleague instead?
brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: Of course. What’s the best way to reach them, and is it OK to say you suggested it?
Happy to. What does your colleague look after, so I can speak to them about the right thing?

brushoffs.delivery: Agree first (“fair enough”) in a warm, downward tone. Then ask one calm, curious question and stop talking.

responses.text: Understood. Is that because everything’s working well, or because there’s no budget at the moment?

skills.title: Call out the elephant
skills.summary: Say the obvious thing out loud — “This is a cold call”, “We’ve never spoken”. It removes the tension instead of pretending it isn’t there.
skills.why: The prospect already knows it’s a sales call. Pretending otherwise makes you sound slippery and sets off their guard. Naming it first feels honest, lowers the pressure and often earns you a few extra seconds.
examples: Hi [Name], it’s [Rep] — I’ll be honest, this is a cold call.
We’ve never spoken before, so I know this is out of the blue.
You don’t know me, and I’m interrupting your day.
I’m guessing you weren’t sitting there hoping a contractor would ring today?
This is a sales call — I’ll be quick.
skills.practice: Say five different openers out loud, each naming the cold call in a different way. Keep them under 8 seconds. Record yourself and listen back for any “um”, “just” or “sorry to bother you”.
skills.mistake: Naming it and then immediately apologising (“Sorry, I know this is a cold call, you’re probably busy…”). Say it once, calmly, then move on.

skills.title: Micro-contracting
skills.summary: Get a small, explicit agreement before moving on. It puts the prospect in control and gives you permission to carry on.
skills.why: People resist being sold to but cooperate when they’re asked. A small “yes” (30 seconds, a couple of questions) turns an interruption into an agreement and makes the next step easier to ask for.
examples: Can I take 30 seconds to tell you why I called, and then you decide if it’s worth carrying on?
I’ll ask a couple of quick questions, and if there’s nothing there, we both get on with our day. OK?
If at any point this sounds like a waste of time, just say so — deal?
Would it be OK if I asked a couple of questions to see if there’s any point us talking?
Give me a minute, and if I haven’t said anything useful, you can hang up. Fair?
skills.practice: Pair up: one says an opener, the other says “go on”. Immediately follow with a micro-contract. Do it back-to-back five times, then swap.
skills.mistake: Asking for time without saying what for. “Have you got a minute?” invites a “no”. Say what you’ll do with the time and what happens if it’s not useful.

skills.title: Name the feeling
skills.summary: Notice and say what the other person might be feeling. “Sounds like you get a lot of these calls.” It lowers their guard.
skills.why: When someone feels heard, resistance drops. Labelling a feeling (“sounds like…”, “it seems like…”) shows you’re listening and lets them correct you, which gets honest information out.
examples: Sounds like you get a lot of these calls.
You sound a bit sceptical — that’s fair.
It sounds like that’s been a real thorn in your side.
I get the sense you’ve been let down by a contractor before.
It sounds like now’s not great timing.
skills.practice: Take the brush-offs in the Scripts tab. For each one, reply with a label (“sounds like…”) instead of a counter-argument, then pause for three seconds.
skills.mistake: Labelling and then arguing. “Sounds like you’re busy — but this will only take a minute!” undoes the whole thing. Label, then stay quiet.

skills.title: Curiosity over pitching
skills.summary: Ask questions that get them talking about their situation instead of explaining what we do.
skills.why: Prospects believe their own words more than yours. Questions that move from situation → problem → consequence let them talk themselves into seeing the cost of doing nothing.
examples: Who looks after your chillers and cooling plant at the moment?
How’s that working out for you?
When was the last unplanned breakdown, and what happened?
What did that end up costing you?
What happens if that doesn’t get sorted?
skills.practice: Run a 3-minute call where you’re not allowed to make a single statement about what we do — questions only. Observer counts statements.
skills.mistake: Interrogating. Asking five questions in a row without acknowledging the answer. Use a short reflection (“OK, so it’s a mix of in-house and contractor”) between questions.

skills.title: Permission to say no
skills.summary: Make “no” a safe answer. It makes “yes” more likely and gets you honest answers. Go further and hunt for the no: word the ask so that “no” means yes.
skills.why: If “no” feels hard, people hedge and brush you off. If it’s explicitly OK, they relax and tell you the truth — and the ones who say yes mean it.
examples: If it’s not relevant, just say so and I’ll leave you alone.
Is that a waste of your time? You can tell me.
If there’s nothing there, I’ll tell you.
It’s fine if it’s not for you — no hard feelings.
Would it be worth 15 minutes, or is it not a priority right now?
Would it be totally unreasonable to suggest a site visit?
skills.practice: Rewrite your usual close so it includes an easy “no”. Say it to a partner and ask them whether it felt pushy.
skills.mistake: Saying it insincerely. If you say “no problem” and then chase, they’ll notice. Mean it — and if they say no, thank them and move on.

voices.name: Direct
voices.summary: Honest, upfront about the cold call, never chases. The prospect decides whether it is relevant. Pattern-interrupt openers that sound nothing like a sales call.
voices.when: Best with senior, time-poor people and anyone who has heard every pitch. Works well for openers and brush-offs.
voices.watch: Can come across as cold if your tone is flat. Keep it warm and relaxed, never aggressive.

voices.name: Curious
voices.summary: Calm, neutral, curious tone. Staged questions (situation, problem, consequence, solution, decision) so the prospect talks themselves into change.
voices.when: Best once someone is on the line and willing to talk. Perfect for engineers and facilities managers who like to explain how things work.
voices.watch: Do not rush the stages. If you jump to the consequence before they have described the problem, it feels like a trap.

voices.name: Structured
voices.summary: Agree the agenda, the time and the possible outcomes up front. Move from the surface problem to the business and personal impact. “No” is always OK.
voices.when: Best for structured meetings and procurement or project people who want clarity. Good for micro-agreements and closes.
voices.watch: Keep it light and conversational on a cold call. Too formal and it sounds scripted.

ladder.name: Research
ladder.purpose: 5 minutes on the company and person: sites, recent news, projects, LinkedIn activity.
ladder.detail: Look for one thing you can reference: a new site, a project, a post, a job change. Write one line in the Pipedrive notes — it’s your door-opener for the call.

ladder.name: LinkedIn connect
ladder.purpose: Connection request with a short, non-salesy note.
ladder.detail: Under 200 characters. No pitch. Make it about them or the sector. If they don’t accept, don’t chase — move on.

ladder.name: LinkedIn engage
ladder.purpose: Like / comment thoughtfully on 2–3 of their posts or company posts.
ladder.detail: The aim is to be familiar before you call. A genuine comment is worth ten likes.

ladder.name: Cold call
ladder.purpose: First voice contact using the core skills.
ladder.detail: Elephant, micro-contract, short reason, curiosity. If no answer, leave a short voicemail and follow with an email.

ladder.name: Cold email
ladder.purpose: Short, plain-text email — sent same day as the call or as a voicemail follow-up.
ladder.detail: Under 100 words, one question, no attachments. Subject line short and lower-case.

ladder.name: Mushroom
ladder.purpose: Find and connect with 2–3 other people in the same organisation (other sites, other functions, other levels).
ladder.detail: One contact is a single point of failure. Map the org: engineering, maintenance, facilities, procurement, ops, energy.

ladder.name: Warm call
ladder.purpose: Follow-up call that references a previous touch.
ladder.detail: Open with the earlier touch: “we connected on LinkedIn”, “I sent you an email on…”. It’s a different call from a cold one.

ladder.name: Warm email
ladder.purpose: Follow-up email adding value (case study, insight, question).
ladder.detail: Give before you ask. One useful thing, one soft question.

ladder.name: Meeting booked
ladder.detail: Confirm in writing, agree the agenda, and tell them what you’ll bring. Keep the remaining cadence tasks cancelled.

ladder.name: Nurture
ladder.purpose: Not now ≠ never. Light touch every 4–6 weeks.
ladder.detail: Value-add emails, LinkedIn likes, an occasional “still on your list?”. Put the next touch in the diary so it doesn’t slip.

cadence.label: Cold email #1 (if no answer, after voicemail)
Mushroom: connect with 2 colleagues at the same company
Call #3 (warm if any reply, otherwise cold)

email: Plain text. No logos, no images, no fancy signature.
One question only — and make it easy to answer.
No attachments on the first email.
Subject line short and lower-case, like an internal email.
Say it’s a cold email if it is. Honesty beats cleverness.
Give a clear way to say no.
linkedin: Connection notes under 200 characters. No pitch.
Engage before you message: like and comment on a few posts first.
After connecting, send value or a question — never a sales pitch.
Comment with substance. “Great post” is invisible.
Post once a week: a lesson, a tip, a site photo or a question.
If they don’t reply to two messages, stop and move to another channel.

mushroom.intro: Mushrooming means growing contacts across an account like a mushroom colony — many small threads under the surface, not one big stem. If your only contact leaves or goes quiet, the account dies. If you have three, it doesn’t.
checklist: Map 3+ contacts per account (different level, function or site).
Add the second and third contact to Pipedrive and link them to the same organisation.
Connect on LinkedIn with each — different note for each.
Reference colleagues only where you’ve genuinely spoken to them (don’t name-drop falsely).
Use referral emails and warm-call openers that reference colleagues.
questions: Who else gets involved when plant decisions are made?
Who looks after this at your other sites?
Who should I speak to so I’m not wasting your time?

training.title: The real problem
training.body: We know who to target. The gap is what “working the client” actually means. Ask the room: “When you say you’re working an account, what have you actually done this week?”

training.title: The Outreach Ladder & Cadence
training.body: Walk through the 10 rungs and the 21-day rhythm. Key message: one call is not a strategy; 8–10 touches across channels is. Introduce mushrooming.

training.title: Skill 1: Call out the elephant
training.body: Why pretending it’s not a cold call makes it worse. Example lines. Pairs say three openers out loud.

training.title: Skill 2: Micro-contracting
training.body: Small agreements, prospect in control. Example lines. Practice: opener + micro-contract back to back.

training.title: Skill 3: Name the feeling
training.body: Label scepticism, busyness, past bad experiences. Practice reacting to brush-offs with a label instead of a counter-argument.

training.title: Skills 4 & 5: Curiosity & permission to say no
training.body: Questions over pitching (situation → problem → consequence). Making “no” safe. Introduce the three conversation styles briefly.

training.title: Live practice
training.body: Pairs/threes: caller, prospect, observer. Real persona cards (e.g. Engineering Director at a food factory, ageing chillers). Rotate. Observer ticks off: elephant / contract / label / question / close.

training.title: Commit & launch the app
training.body: Everyone installs the app, adds their 5 real prospects to Pipedrive, sets their call days. Agree team targets for the next two weeks and a review date.
